cards.title: Prioritize A/B tests by recipient volume, not by ease
cards.summary: Focus split tests on the emails and flows in your account that reach the most recipients so any win compounds across revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email or flow to test next when you can only run a limited number of experiments per month on your store's lifecycle program.
steps: Map each flow and campaign to its monthly recipient volume and revenue contribution before choosing a test target.
Rank the biggest levers first: welcome series, abandoned checkout, abandoned cart, and post-purchase/winback flows, plus the first 2-3 emails of each.
Within those, test high-recipient emails before testing minor flows that only reach tens of recipients per month.
Treat improvements on a 20-recipient flow as marginal: it may lift that flow's conversion, but it will not move overall store revenue materially.
Allocate test slots so at least the majority of experiments land on the top flows and top campaign sends.
caveats: The source frames this as advice for general ecommerce stores, especially under roughly $100K/month; large multi-million-dollar stores can afford to chase smaller levers.
Recipient volume ranking depends on your own account data, not a fixed universal list.

cards.title: Test send time against place order rate, not open rate
cards.summary: Run send-time split tests with place order rate as the winning metric because the hour with the best open rate is often not the hour with the most orders.
cards.use_when: Scheduling campaign sends and deciding whether to trust Klaviyo's Smart Send Time or run your own send-time test.
steps: Create an A/B test on the campaign and choose 'test send time' rather than relying only on Smart Send Time.
Pick two clearly different times (for example 7 a.m. versus 7 p.m.) to start with a meaningful contrast.
In the test settings, set the winning metric to place order rate, not click rate and definitely not open rate, since revenue and placed orders are the KPIs that matter.
Keep size distribution at 100 and track links separately per variation so you can attribute results correctly.
Run the comparison across roughly 5-10 campaigns before concluding; one campaign is effectively zero data.
Once a winner emerges, narrow the test (for example 7 a.m. versus 11 a.m., then 11 a.m. versus 2 p.m.) to pinpoint the best window.
caveats: The source states it has repeatedly seen the best open-rate time differ from the best place-order time, but notes this is not universal across all brands.
The 5-10 campaign range is a heuristic that depends on audience size and revenue level, not a fixed rule.

cards.title: Test content structure in campaigns, not just subject lines
cards.summary: Run campaign content tests (product blocks vs none, bestsellers vs categories) because the learning transfers to flows and future sends, unlike one-off subject line tests.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign experiments and choosing which content variables to vary in your store's promotional and evergreen sends.
steps: Set up an A/B test on content rather than only on subject lines, since subject-line results on a one-time campaign cannot be reused elsewhere.
Version A: original email with product blocks. Version B: same email without product blocks. Compare results.
Run a second variant type on sitewide sales: one version highlighting three bestsellers versus one version highlighting product categories or new arrivals.
Set the winning metric to place order rate where possible; the source notes Klaviyo does not allow place order rate for subject-line tests, so click rate is the next-best option there.
Run each content test across multiple campaigns before drawing conclusions and before applying the pattern to flows.
caveats: Subject-line tests on one-off campaigns yield data you cannot act on elsewhere; the source recommends deprioritizing them for that reason.
Place order rate is not selectable as a winner metric for all test types in Klaviyo; verify the current interface.

cards.title: Use 50/50 manual distribution for email A/B tests
cards.summary: Turn off Klaviyo's automatic distribution and split traffic 50/50 so you keep control of the test and have enough data for a sound winner decision.
cards.use_when: Configuring test settings for subject line or content A/B tests in campaigns and flows.
steps: In the test settings, turn off 'automatically chosen distribution' and set the split manually to 50/50.
Expect automatic distribution to shift more sends toward whichever variant Klaviyo currently favors, which can bias the comparison.
Accept the tradeoff: manual 50/50 requires you to check and analyze the test yourself, which the source's agency prefers because it wants full control.
If you lack time to monitor tests, the source says enabling automatic distribution is acceptable.
For winner selection, the default is click rate; configure to open rate if needed, but note place order rate is not available for subject-line tests, and click rate is the better fallback.
Leave the winner-selection method on 'test by statistical significance' or choose the time limit; alternatively switch it off and pick the winner manually.
Write a note on the test explaining your hypothesis so you can interpret it later.
caveats: These are the source's stated preferences from agency practice, not universal requirements.
Automatic distribution behavior and test-setting labels in Klaviyo may change; verify the current interface.

cards.title: A/B test abandonment flow timing with conditional splits
cards.summary: Test the delay before your abandoned cart and abandoned browse emails by building two flow paths with different wait times, then narrow toward the best delay.
cards.use_when: Optimizing abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, or browse abandonment flow timing to lift placed orders while watching spam complaint rate.
steps: Add a conditional split at the top of the flow and set the condition to a random sample of 50%.
Set the 'yes' path to one delay (for example 2 hours) and the 'no' path to another (for example 1 hour) so the difference at the start is meaningful.

Duplicate every email so each path carries the full sequence rather than rejoining after the first email; the source prefers this because email 1 may perform worse at the longer delay while emails 2-3 perform better, and you want the full picture.
After results come in, narrow the comparison (for example test 2 hours versus 3 hours) to pinpoint the ideal delay.
Monitor spam complaint rate alongside placed order rate, since timing changes affect both.
Repeat the same conditional-split approach for browse abandonment, starting with a wider gap such as 1 hour versus 3 hours.
caveats: Splitting every email into two paths multiplies maintenance work; the source prefers it for full-sequence visibility, but it is a tradeoff.
Ideal delays are store-specific; the 1/2/3/4-hour values are illustrative test values, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Flow subject lines are worth testing, campaign subject lines usually are not
cards.summary: Test subject lines in flows because they run indefinitely, but deprioritize campaign subject-line tests whose results you cannot reuse.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend subject-line testing effort across your welcome, abandonment, and post-purchase flows versus one-time campaigns.
steps: For flow emails, go to the email you want to test, hit 'create a test', and enter an alternative subject line (for example 'did you see something you liked' versus 'oops you forgot something').
Run the subject-line test on flows because they send continuously, so a winning line keeps producing results over time.
For campaigns, treat subject-line testing as low-value: the send is one-time, so a winner gives you little actionable information afterward.
Instead of campaign subject lines, direct campaign test effort toward send times and content variations that inform your flows and future campaigns.
Still set the winning metric responsibly: use click rate when place order rate is not selectable.
caveats: This is the source's stated preference and a judgment about actionability, not a claim that subject lines never matter.
Klaviyo's test-creation flow and available metrics may change; verify the current interface.

cards.title: Skip CTA-color split tests at small store scale
cards.summary: Button-color A/B tests (yellow vs red) are generally not worth running for stores under roughly $100K/month because the expected lift is too small.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate limited testing capacity for a small or mid-size store's email program, signup forms, or above-the-fold email content.
steps: Recognize that CTA color tests usually show meaningful differences only for very large senders, in the source's experience brands doing multiple millions per month with very large audiences.
For stores under about $100K/month, redirect that test slot to bigger levers: flow timing, content structure, and first-email variants in top flows.
If you do test above-the-fold email content, test headlines and calls to action rather than only button color.
Note that color tests are technically possible and can produce a difference; the source's position is that the gain is minor relative to effort at small scale.
caveats: The ~$100K/month threshold and the 'millions per month' scale are the source's heuristics based on agency observation, not measured benchmarks.
A large-audience brand may legitimately find color tests worthwhile.

cards.title: Write email copy that earns attention through value, not cleverness alone
cards.summary: Voice and personality make copy less robotic, but value to the reader is what drives response; build the email around a clear, useful offer first.
cards.use_when: Drafting campaign or flow email copy for product launches, promos, or category sales that need to fit your brand voice.
steps: Lead with value: the source frames value as more than half the battle, with tone and formatting tips finishing the job.
Make the headline immediately clear about what the reader gets, for example a percent-off product sale, so attention is grabbed by clarity as well as offers.

Write body copy in the brand's voice rather than generic promo language; a line that is a little edgy or funny fits a brand like Dollar Shave Club, whereas a generic 'hurry, selling out fast' line can convert but fits worse.
Call out the discount code explicitly and pair it with a clear call-to-action button such as 'save now'.
Insert recommended product blocks, then close with body copy that continues the same on-brand tone rather than reverting to generic urgency.
Keep sentences short and snappy as a finishing pass after the value and voice are right.
caveats: The Dollar Shave Club example is the source's constructed demo, not a measured performance case study.
Brand-voice edginess is not a universal rule; a generic line may still convert.

cards.title: Structure promo emails around headline, code, CTA, products, and closing copy
cards.summary: A tested promotional email layout moves from a clear attention-grabbing headline through an explicit discount code and CTA to recommended products and on-brand closing copy.
cards.use_when: Building the layout and copy order for a discount or category-sale email in your store's campaign calendar.
steps: Open with an attention-grabbing headline that makes the offer immediately clear, such as '20% off shower products'.
Follow with body copy written in your brand's tone so the email reads as a fit for your audience rather than a template.
State the discount code prominently and place a clear call-to-action button, for example 'save now'.
Add 'recommended for you' product blocks so recipients can act on the offer without leaving the email's context.
Close with additional body copy that reinforces the sale and repeats the code, keeping the same voice throughout.
Compare your draft against the generic alternative (plain percent-off plus urgency) to check whether your version is genuinely more on-brand.
caveats: This layout comes from the source's demo campaign, not from a documented A/B test result.
A generic urgency line may perform acceptably; brand fit is the differentiator the source argues for.

cards.title: Track place order rate as the primary email KPI hierarchy
cards.summary: Optimize emails for revenue and place order rate first, then click rate, and treat open rate as the least important metric in the chain.
cards.use_when: Choosing the winning metric for any email A/B test or deciding which send-time or content variant to adopt in your store.
steps: Set revenue and place order rate as the top-level KPIs for email decisions.
Rank click rate second and open rate last, since higher opens do not reliably translate to more orders.
When comparing send times or content variants, prefer the option producing more placed orders even if its open rate is lower.
Where a platform does not allow place order rate as the winner metric (the source notes this limitation for subject-line tests in Klaviyo), fall back to click rate rather than open rate.
Check the platform's current metric options before configuring, since available selections can change.
caveats: The source reports that the best open-rate time often differs from the best place-order time, but this is agency observation rather than a universal law.
Metric availability in Klaviyo varies by test type.

cards.title: Sequence send-time tests from wide contrast to narrow pinpointing
cards.summary: Find your best send time by first testing two very different hours, then progressively narrowing around the winner across multiple campaigns.
cards.use_when: Establishing a default campaign send time for your store instead of relying on a single Smart Send Time suggestion.
steps: Start with a wide contrast between the two test times so any real difference is detectable.
Let the test run across several campaigns (the source suggests roughly 5-10) rather than judging from one send.
Take the winning hour and pair it against a neighboring hour in the next round, for example 7 a.m. versus 11 a.m.
Repeat with a progressively tighter bracket, for example 11 a.m. versus 2 p.m., converging on the best window.
Apply the resulting send time as your default, but keep monitoring place order rate rather than assuming the optimum is fixed.
caveats: The number of campaigns needed scales with audience size and revenue in the source's framing; 5-10 is a heuristic.
Results are brand-specific and may shift with seasonality or list changes.

cards.title: Expect to customize templates to your brand instead of copying them
cards.summary: Templates and flows give you a starting blueprint, but each store must test which retargeting flows, designs, and campaigns its own customers respond to.
cards.use_when: Rolling out a new email program or onboarding templates into your store and setting realistic expectations for iteration.
steps: Treat any provided template as a starting point, not a finished system; the source states not every template will fit a brand's needs.
Determine through testing which flows retarget your customers best, which email design engages them most, and which campaigns they want to see.
Accept trial and error as part of finding the right system, strategy, design, and flows for your specific store.
Prioritize iteration on high-recipient flows and sends so your trial and error produces compounding learning.
caveats: The source promotes a paid service with a stated 20% revenue guarantee in 60 days; such claims are the presenter's marketing and are not independent evidence.
No specific template or design is guaranteed to fit a given store.
